viewpoint: Large language models (LLMs) can generate intermediate chain of thought (CoT) reasoning steps to perform complex reasoning in few- and zero-shot settings.
Each reasoning step generated by LLMs can rely on external tools to support computation beyond the core LLM capabilities.
Prior work on CoT prompting and tool use often requires hand-crafting task-specific demonstrations and carefully scripted interleaving of model generations with tool use.
We have introduced Automatic Reasoning and Tool-use (ART), a framework that uses frozen LLMs to automatically generate intermediate reasoning steps as a program.
Given a new task to solve, ART selects demonstrations of multi-step reasoning and tool use from a task library. (It doesn't specify how these demonstrations are used to solve the new task)
At test time, ART pauses the generation of intermediate reasoning steps whenever external tools are called, integrates their output, and resumes the generation.

ART significantly outperforms few-shot prompting and automatic CoT on unseen tasks in the BigBench and MMLU benchmarks, and matches the performance of hand-crafted CoT prompts on a majority of these tasks.

ART is flexible, allowing humans to improve its performance by correcting errors in task-specific programs or incorporating new tools, as demonstrated by significantly improving performance on select tasks with minimal human intervention.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have limitations in performing complex tasks that require arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning.
Reasoning frameworks like ReAct, Chain-of-thought (CoT), Tree-of-thoughts (ToT), etc. have shown success in some complex tasks but have limitations in solving long-form complex tasks.
A knowledge-sharing and collaborative multi-agent assisted framework is proposed to address the limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs) in performing complex tasks.
The proposed framework makes use of existing reasoning frameworks and the collaborative skills of multi-agent systems (MASs).

The objectives of the proposed framework are to overcome the limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex tasks, to enhance their reasoning capabilities, and to improve their performance in complex tasks.

The proposed framework involves generating natural language rationales and in-context few-shot learning via prompting, integrates reasoning techniques, and utilizes efficient knowledge-sharing and communication-driven agent networks.

The proposed framework could lead to benefits such as saving time and money, improved efficiency for computationally intensive reasoning, and the ability to incorporate multiple collaboration strategies for dynamically changing environments.
Human intelligence benefits from cognitive synergy, where collaboration among multiple minds creates superior outcomes compared to isolated individuals.
The proposed Solo Performance Prompting (SPP) technique converts a single Language Model (LLM) into a cognitive synergist by means of multi-turn self-collaboration with numerous personas.
A cognitive synergist is an intelligent agent that combines the strengths and knowledge of multiple minds to improve problem-solving in complex tasks.
The proposed SPP transforms a single LLM into an intelligent agent capable of enhancing complex problem-solving through collaboration among multiple minds.
By dynamically identifying and simulating various personas based on task inputs, SPP unlocks the potential of cognitive synergy in LLMs.
Our analysis shows that having multiple, fine-grained personas in LLMs enhances problem-solving abilities compared to using just a single or a fixed number of personas.

Solo Performance Prompting (SPP) was evaluated on three complex tasks: Trivia Creative Writing, Codenames Collaborative, and Logic Grid Puzzle, which span both knowledge-intensive and reasoning-intensive task types.

In contrast to previous works such as Chain-of-Thought that only increase reasoning abilities in LLMs, experimental results indicate that SPP effectively reduces factual hallucination and maintains robust reasoning capabilities.

Additional comparative experiments show that cognitive synergy occurs exclusively in GPT-4 and not in less capable models, such as GPT-3.5-turbo and Llama2-13b-chat, which parallels the development of human cognition.
Links to code, data, and prompts for Solo Performance Prompting (SPP) can be found at the provided GitHub repository.
Large Language Models have revolutionized Natural Language Processing.
Large Language Models exhibit limitations in autonomously addressing novel challenges such as reasoning and problem-solving.
Traditional techniques like chain-of-thought prompting necessitate explicit human guidance.
A novel multi-agent communication framework is introduced to enhance LLMs' autonomous problem-solving capabilities.
The multi-agent communication framework is inspired by the CAMEL model.
The framework employs multiple LLM agents.
Each LLM agent has a distinct persona.
The multiple LLM agents engage in role-playing communication.
The multi-agent communication approach offers a nuanced and adaptable approach to diverse problem scenarios.
Extensive experimentation is conducted to demonstrate the framework's superior performance and adaptability.
The collaborative potential of multiple agents is investigated in overcoming the limitations of individual models.
Insights are provided into the collaborative potential of multiple agents.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting is a method that offers step-by-step problem-solving rationales for large language models (LLMs).
The standard Chain-of-thought (CoT) method is less effective for problems requiring multiple reasoning steps.

The complexity of multi-step problems is the cause of the limitation of the standard Chain-of-thought (CoT) method. The later reasoning stages in multi-step problems depend on the results of several steps earlier, not just the immediately preceding step.
The complexities in multi-step problems imply that the reasoning process can be effectively represented as a graph.
The almost linear and straightforward structure of Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting struggles to capture the complex reasoning graph inherent in multi-step problems.

To overcome the limitations in multi-step reasoning with Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, we propose Residual Connection Prompting (RESPROMPT) as a new prompting strategy for large language models (LLMs).
Our main idea is to restructure the reasoning graph within the prompts for the large language models (LLMs).
We reconstruct the reasoning graph within the prompts by integrating crucial connections-links that are present in the reasoning graph but missing in the linear Chain-of-thought (CoT) flow.

The missing connections in the linear CoT flow, termed "residual connections", play an essential role in transforming the structure into a graph representation, effectively capturing the complex reasoning graphs present in multi-step problems.
We test the effectiveness of RESPROMPT on six benchmarks in three diverse domains: math, sequential, and commonsense reasoning.
On the open-sourced LLaMA family of models, RESPROMPT resulted in a significant average reasoning accuracy improvement of 12.5% on LLaMA-65B and 6.8% on LLaMA2-70B.

Further analysis reveals that RESPROMPT performs exceptionally well in complex multi-step reasoning problems. RESPROMPT outperforms the best Chain-of-thought (CoT) based benchmarks, resulting in an average improvement of 21.1% on LLaMA-65B and 14.3% on LLaMA2-70B for questions requiring at least five reasoning steps.
We identify the most effective way to build residual connections through comprehensive ablation studies and analyses.
Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks.
A new decoding strategy, called self-consistency, is proposed in this paper to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting.

The self-consistency decoding strategy first samples diverse sets of reasoning paths, rather than choosing only the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths.
Self-consistency decoding strategy uses the intuition that complex reasoning problems often admit multiple alternative thinking approaches leading to their correct answer.
Large language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language generation, understanding, and few-shot learning in recent years.
An extensive body of work has explored improving the performance of large language models using prompting tools, such as verification, self-consistency, or intermediate scratchpads.

In this paper, we propose a method to improve language responses by having multiple language model instances propose, debate, and then reach a consensus on individual responses and reasoning processes through multiple rounds.
This approach, when applied to language models, results in a common final answer.
Our findings show that the proposed approach significantly improves mathematical and strategic reasoning across multiple tasks.
We find that our approach reduces fallacious answers and hallucinations that are common in contemporary language models when generating content.
Our approach can be applied directly to existing black-box language models, and it uses the same procedure and prompts for all tasks that we investigate.

Our findings suggest that the "society of minds" approach has the potential to significantly advance the capabilities of large language models and lead to breakthroughs in language generation and understanding.
Pre-trained Language Models internalize a great amount of world knowledge.
Pre-trained Language Models have been shown incapable of recalling world knowledge to solve tasks requiring complex & multi-step reasoning.
Humans develop a “chain of thought” to solve tasks requiring complex & multi-step reasoning.
It is necessary to equip Pre-trained Language Models with the ability to develop a "chain of thought" for these tasks.
An iterative prompting framework is explored in this work.
A new prompting paradigm is proposed that prompts Pre-trained Language Models to progressively elicit relevant knowledge for multi-step inference.
Key limitations of existing prompting methods are identified.
Existing prompting methods are restricted to queries with only a single identifiable relation/predicate.
Existing prompting methods are agnostic to input contexts, making it challenging to handle variations across multiple inference steps.
An iterative context-aware prompter is proposed that can adapt prompts conditioned on the current step’s contexts, addressing the limitations of existing prompting methods.
The effectiveness of the iterative scheme and the context-aware prompter design is demonstrated through experiments on three datasets involving multi-step reasoning.
Recent advancements in large language models have led to improvements in methods that elicit reasoning chains for solving reasoning tasks.
Tasks requiring multiple steps of reasoning are still challenging for state-of-the-art models.
Our proposed method, PathFinder, is inspired by the beam search algorithm and is a tree-search-based reasoning path generation approach.
PathFinder enhances diverse branching and multi-hop reasoning through the use of dynamic decoding, which is enabled by varying sampling methods and parameters.
PathFinder uses constrained reasoning, which includes novel quality constraints, pruning, and exploration methods to improve the efficiency and the quality of generated reasoning paths.
PathFinder includes scoring and ranking features to improve the selection of candidate reasoning paths.
Our proposed method, PathFinder, outperforms competitive baselines by 6% on average in solving three complex arithmetic and commonsense reasoning tasks.
Our proposed model, PathFinder, generalizes well to longer, unseen reasoning chains and exhibits similar complexities to beam search with large branching factors.
Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) internalize a great amount of world knowledge.
Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) are shown incapable of recalling these world knowledge to solve tasks requiring complex & multi-step inference procedures.
There is a need to equip Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) with the abilities to develop a “train of thought” for tasks requiring complex & multi-step inference.

The work explores an iterative prompting framework, a new prompting paradigm designed to progressively obtain relevant knowledge from Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) for multi-step inference tasks.
There are limitations with existing prompting methods used for multi-step inference tasks with Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs).

Existing prompting methods for multi-step inference tasks with Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) either restrict queries to single identifiable relations/predicate or are agnostic to input contexts, making it difficult to capture variations in abilities across different inference steps.
The proposed solution is an iterative context-aware prompter, designed to address limitations in existing methods by learning to dynamically synthesize prompts based on the current step’s contexts.
Experiments on three datasets involving multi-step inference tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed iterative scheme and the context-aware prompter design.
The experiments demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness and the paper presents results on three multi-step inference datasets
Large language models face criticisms for biases, hallucinations, and a lack of reasoning capability.
The paper introduces SocraSynth, a multi-LLM agent platform to address the issues of biases, hallucinations, and reasoning capability in LLMs.
SocraSynth utilizes conditional statistics, systematic context enhancement, and adjustable debate contentiousness levels to mitigate the issues in LLMs.
SocraSynth typically involves a human moderator and two LLM agents, each representing an opposing viewpoint on a given subject.
SocraSynth operates in two main stages: knowledge generation and reasoning evaluation.
During the knowledge generation phase, the moderator sets the debate topic and contentiousness level, and the agents create supporting arguments based on their respective viewpoints.
During the reasoning evaluation phase, Socratic reasoning and formal logic principles are used to assess the quality of the arguments presented.
The dialogue ends with the moderator adjusting the contentiousness level, encouraging cooperation, and gathering concluding remarks to facilitate human decision-making.
The paper demonstrates SocraSynth's ability to promote rigorous research, dynamic reasoning, comprehensive assessment, and collaboration through case studies in three distinct application domains.
Multi-agent interactions using LLMs are valuable for advanced knowledge extraction and decision-making support, according to this paper.
Generating a chain of thought -- a series of intermediate reasoning steps -- significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning.

Reasoning abilities emerge naturally in sufficiently large language models via a simple method called chain of thought prompting, which involves providing a few chain of thought demonstrations as exemplars in prompting.
Chain of thought prompting improves performance on a range of arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks, according to experiments on three large language models.

Prompting a 540B-parameter language model with just eight chain of thought exemplars achieves state of the art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing even a finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier.
Chain-of-thought prompting has excellent performance on natural language reasoning tasks.
Chain-of-thought prompting struggles on problems harder than the examples provided in the prompts.
The performance of chain-of-thought prompting degrades for problems harder than the examples provided.
A new prompting strategy, least-to-most prompting, is proposed to address the easy-to-hard generalization challenge faced by chain-of-thought prompting.
Least-to-most prompting strategy involves breaking a complex problem into a series of subproblems and solving them successively.
The solutions to each subproblem depend on the solutions to the previous subproblems in the sequence.

Experimental findings reveal that least-to-most prompting successfully generalizes to harder problems than those presented in the prompts across tasks such as symbolic manipulation, compositional generalization, and math reasoning.

The GPT-3 model with least-to-most prompting solves the SCAN compositional generalization benchmark for any split (including length split) with high accuracy (99%) using only 14 examples, which is significantly better than the 16% accuracy with chain-of-thought prompting.

The use of least-to-most prompting improves the performance of the GPT-3 model on compositional generalization task by achieving 99% accuracy using fewer examples compared to chain-of-thought prompting.

Improved performance achieved with least-to-most prompting is significant considering that neural-symbolic models specialized in solving SCAN are usually trained on a large dataset of over 15,000 examples.

The 99% accuracy achieved by the GPT-3 model using 14 examples is particularly remarkable given that specialized neural-symbolic models trained on 15,000+ examples only attain similar performance on SCAN.
A set of prompts for various tasks related to symbolic manipulation, compositional generalization, and math reasoning have been provided in the Appendix.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in reasoning tasks.
The development of prompting methods has contributed to LLMs' success in reasoning tasks.
Existing prompting approaches cannot reuse insights from solving similar problems.
Existing prompting approaches suffer from accumulated errors in multi-step reasoning.
These issues arise because the existing prompting approaches ask LLMs to reason from scratch for each problem.
We propose \textit{Thought Propagation} (TP) as a solution to the issues in existing prompting approaches.
Thought Propagation explores analogous problems to enhance LLMs' complex reasoning ability.
Thought Propagation leverages solutions from analogous problems to improve LLMs' reasoning ability.
Analogous problems are linked to the input problem.
The solutions and problem-solving strategies of analogous problems can be reused to solve the input problem.
Propagating insights from solving previous analogous problems is a promising approach to inspiring new problem-solving.
To enhance LLMs' reasoning ability, TP first prompts them to propose and solve a set of analogous problems.
The set of solutions from analogous problems is used to enhance LLMs' reasoning ability.
TP asks LLMs to propose and solve analogous problems to the input problem to achieve this.
TP reuses the results of analogous problems to directly yield a solution or derive a plan for execution.
This approach uses the insights from previous analogous problems to improve the initial solution obtained from scratch.
TP is compatible with existing prompting approaches, making it easy to implement and enhance reasoning in various tasks without significant effort.
This compatibility allows TP to extend existing prompting approaches without requiring extensive task-specific prompt engineering.
TP shows substantial improvement in three challenging tasks.
In Shortest-path Reasoning, TP achieves a 12\% absolute increase in finding the optimal solutions.
In Creative Writing, TP improves human preference by 13\%.
In the LLM-Agent Planning task, TP boosts the task completion rate by 15\%.
Large Language Models (LLMs) prompted to generate chain-of-thought (CoT) exhibit impressive reasoning capabilities.
Recent attempts at solving complex, multi-step reasoning problems depend on the ability of LLMs to both decompose and solve the problems simultaneously.
Adapting foundational LLMs through fine-tuning is computationally prohibitive due to their unavailability.

The ability to decompose complex problems into subproblems and generate solutions is considered distinct capabilities, that are better addressed in separate modules rather than a single monolithic LLM.
Our method believes (and demonstrates) this.
We introduce DaSLaM, a method that uses a decomposition generator to transform complex problems into smaller, easier-to-solve subproblems.
These subproblems require fewer reasoning steps.
The answers to the decomposed subproblems are provided by the solver.

We use a small LLM (with 13B parameters) as the decomposition generator in our method. This LLM is trained using policy gradient optimization to cooperate with a solver LM (regarded as a black box) and assist it through each subproblem.
Our approach is solver-agnostic as a result.

Evaluation of our method on multiple different reasoning datasets shows that a 175 billion parameter LLM (text-davinci-003) can produce competitive or even better performance than its larger successor, GPT-4.

We demonstrate that our modular approach is not limited by the solver's capabilities, no matter the scale, as it provides significant performance improvement with our solver-agnostic decomposition technique. For instance, LMs with various sizes serve as solvers and give a substantial boost to the performance.
Extensive analyses of our method reveal the superiority of our modular fine-tuning technique over exceptionally large decomposer LLMs that only utilize prompting.
In open-domain question-answering (ODQA), most questions require single-hop reasoning on commonsense.
We officially introduce open-domain multi-hop reasoning (ODMR) to answer multi-hop questions with explicit reasoning steps in open-domain setting.
Recently, LLMs have found significant utility in facilitating ODQA without external corpus.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting significantly boosts the reasoning capability of LLMs with both manual and automated paradigms.
Existing automated methods lack quality assurance, and manual approaches suffer from limited scalability and poor diversity, hindering the capabilities of LLMs in ODMR.
We propose Self-prompted Chain-of-Thought (SP-CoT), an automated framework to generate high-quality CoTs of LLMs using LLMs.
SP-CoT introduces an automated pipeline for generating high-quality ODMR datasets, an adaptive sampler for selecting CoT in context, and self-prompted inference using in-context learning.

Our proposed SP-CoT significantly outperforms previous SOTA methods on large-scale (175B) LLMs, and nearly doubles the zero-shot performance of small-scale (13B) LLMs on four multi-hop question-answering benchmarks.
Further analysis demonstrates that SP-CoT can efficiently generate direct and concise intermediate reasoning steps by recalling $\sim$50\% of intermediate answers on the MuSiQue-Ans dataset.
Modern large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have shown remarkable performance on general language tasks.
Modern large language models (LLMs) still struggle on complex reasoning tasks.
The research on cognitive behaviors of LLMs is driven by the need to explore human-like problem-solving strategies.
One representative strategy for exploring human-like problem-solving strategies in LLMs is self-reflection.
Our study shows that reflection-style methods suffer from the Degeneration-of-Thought (DoT) problem.
A Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework is proposed to address the Degeneration-of-Thought (DoT) problem.
The Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework involves multiple agents and a judge, with the agents expressing their arguments and the judge managing the debate process.
The Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework encourages divergent thinking in LLMs, which is helpful for tasks that require deep levels of contemplation.
The Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework was effective in solving commonsense machine translation and counter-intuitive arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Good performance of the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework requires adaptive breaks in the debate and a modest level of "tit for tat" state.
It is not recommended to use different LLMs as judges if they will also serve as agents within the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework.
The Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) framework code is available at this URL: https://github.com/Skytliang/Multi-Agents-Debate
The performance of in-context learning with large language models (LLMs) is gaining attention due to its strong few-shot performance on various tasks.
The performance of LLMs on text-to-SQL parsing needs improvement.
Improving the multi-step reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) may help with text-to-SQL parsing performance.
This paper explores methods to boost large language models' (LLMs) multi-step reasoning ability using chain of thought (CoT) prompting techniques.
Experiments show that iterative CoT-style prompting may not be necessary for text-to-SQL parsing, as presented in Zhou et al. (2023).
Using detailed reasoning steps in CoT-style prompting may lead to more error propagation issues in text-to-SQL parsing.
A new CoT-style prompting method is proposed to address the issues found in text-to-SQL parsing.
The proposed method achieves: 5.2 absolute gains on the Spider development set and 6.5 absolute gains on the Spider Realistic set over the standard prompting method without reasoning steps;

The proposed method also attains: 2.4 absolute gains compared to the least-to-most prompting method on the Spider development set and 1.5 absolute gains compared to the least-to-most prompting method on the Spider Realistic set.
The task of interests is prompting large-scale language models to perform multi-step reasoning.
Existing work shows that language models can generate new reasoning chains from CoT sequences.
A central question is determining the most effective reasoning examples for prompts.
In this work, we propose complexity-based prompting as a simple and effective example selection process for multi-step reasoning.
We demonstrate that prompts with higher reasoning complexity lead to better performance on multi-step reasoning tasks.
We also apply the reasoning complexity criteria to the decoding in selecting outputs.
Our approach significantly improves multi-step reasoning accuracy on several math benchmarks and tasks after prompting GPT-3 and Codex.
The average improvement in accuracy is +5.3 and a maximum of +18.
Selection based on reasoning complexity is shown to be intuitive, easy to implement, and annotation-efficient compared to existing example selection schemes.
Performance gains from complex prompts are demonstrated to be robust under format perturbation and distribution shift.
Step-Back Prompting is a simple technique to enable large language models (LLMs) to derive high-level concepts and first principles from specific instances.
Using the derived high-level concepts and first principles, LLMs can significantly improve their ability to follow a correct reasoning path towards a solution.
The performance of Step-Back Prompting is evaluated on various challenging reasoning-intensive tasks with the PaLM-2L, GPT-4, and Llama2-70B models.
Substantial performance gains are observed for Step-Back Prompting on reasoning-intensive tasks such as STEM, Knowledge QA, and Multi-Hop Reasoning.
For example, Step-Back Prompting improves the performance of PaLM-2L on MMLU (Physics and Chemistry) by 7% and 11% respectively, TimeQA by 27%, and MuSiQue by 7%.
Large Language Models (LLMs) employing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can improve multi-step reasoning capabilities.
Multi-step reasoning can be divided into two phases: path generation and answer calibration.
We present a summary of recent answer calibration techniques, categorizing them into step-level and path-level strategies for multi-step reasoning.
We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the step-level and path-level answer calibration strategies, assessing their performance across multiple reasoning paths for multi-step reasoning.
The experimental results indicate that optimally combining step-level and path-level answer calibration strategies tends to produce the best outcomes for multi-step reasoning.
This study has the potential to reveal significant insights for optimizing multi-step reasoning through answer calibration.
LLMs can achieve highly effective performance on various reasoning tasks by utilizing chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting as demonstrations in their decision-making process.
The reasoning chains of demonstrations used by LLMs can be prone to errors, which can lead to incorrect reasoning during the inference process.
Using inappropriate exemplars (overly simplistic or complex demos) can have a negative impact on the overall performance of LLMs across varying levels of difficulty.
We propose Iter-CoT, an iterative bootstrapping method designed for selecting exemplars and generating reasoning chains for LLMs.
By employing iterative bootstrapping, our approach allows LLMs to autonomously correct errors, consequently resulting in more precise and comprehensive reasoning chains.

Concurrently, our approach identifies challenging yet answerable questions accompanied by reasoning chains to serve as exemplars. This process ensures a moderate level of difficulty, enhancing the LLMs' generalizability across varying levels of difficulty.
Our experimental results show that Iter-CoT exhibits superiority, achieving competitive performance across three distinct reasoning tasks on ten datasets.

Experimental results demonstrate that Iter-CoT outperforms other methods, maintaining competitive performance in three different reasoning tasks using ten datasets.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has improved the multi-step reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by creating a series of rationales before the answer.

We investigate the reasoning paths produced by CoT and discover two obstacles in multi-step reasoning: (i) producing rationales that are not related to the question, (ii) failing to create subquestions or queries to obtain all the necessary information.
We suggest a graph-guided CoT prompting method to assist Large Language Models (LLMs) in finding the correct answer using graph representation/verification steps.

More specifically, we use Large Language Models (LLMs) to create a "question/rationale graph" from the initial question and the rationales produced in the previous steps with the help of knowledge extraction prompting.

After that, the graph verification step assesses the current rationale triplet against the existing question/rationale graph to eliminate irrelevant rationales and generate additional questions to acquire crucial information.
Furthermore, we develop CoT paths that don't include the obtained graph information to show the context details that were missed during the graph extraction.
Our graph-guided reasoning approach demonstrates better performance compared to past CoT prompting and the variants on multi-hop question answering benchmark datasets.
Many NLP tasks involve selecting the correct answer from multiple options based on implicit knowledge.
Large PLMs can achieve near-human performance on commonsense reasoning tasks, but they provide little human-interpretable evidence of the reasoning process.

This work demonstrates a method to use PLMs to produce evidence of the reasoning used to solve NLP tasks by generating contrastive explanations that highlight the key attributes necessary to justify the correct answer.
Conditioning a model's decisions on the contrastive explanations improves performance on two NLP tasks that involve commonsense reasoning, as compared to previous non-contrastive alternatives.
These contrastive explanations are considered more relevant by humans for solving the task, and they enable a novel method for evaluating explanation faithfulfness.
Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized NLP.
The ability of Large language models (LLMs) to reason is a larger question.
This paper studies the ability of Large language models (LLMs) to reason, specifically focused on math word problems (MWPs) using symbolic versions of the problems.
The symbolic expression is considered a "concise explanation" of the numeric answer.
We create and use a symbolic version of the SVAMP dataset for our study.
The GPT-3's davinci-002 model has good zero-shot accuracy on symbolic math word problems (MWPs).
We evaluate the faithfulness of the model's reasoning by going beyond accuracy and analyzing the alignment between the final answer and the outputted reasoning for symbolic math word problems (MWPs).
The final answer and the outputted reasoning correspond to numeric and symbolic answers for math word problems (MWPs).
We explore a self-prompting approach to encourage the symbolic reasoning of Large language models (LLMs) to align with the numeric answer.
The self-prompting approach enhances the LLM's ability to provide concise and verifiable reasoning for math word problems (MWPs) and increases interpretability.
Surprisingly, self-prompting improves the symbolic accuracy, exceeding both the numeric and symbolic accuracies, which serves as an ensembling effect.
The SVAMP_Sym dataset, containing symbolic math problems, will be released for future research.
Reasoning proofs generated by LLMs are uncertain due to their inherent defects.
We present a neuro-symbolic integration method to address the deficiencies in LLMs.
A neural LLM is used to represent the problem's knowledge in the proposed method.
An LLM-free symbolic solver is used for deliberative reasoning based on the problem's knowledge.
Our method uses customized meta-interpreters to generate reasoning proofs and provide flexible search strategies.
Reasoning proofs are ensured to be causal and reliable due to the deterministic executing nature of the symbolic solvers.
On ProofWriter, our method achieves higher accuracy and greater proof similarity compared to the CoT baseline.
On GSM8K, our method demonstrates improvements in accuracy and nearly double proof similarity.
Our code for the proposed method has been publicly released.
Augmented Language Models combine the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models with tools for knowledge retrieval and action execution.
Existing ALM systems prompt Large Language Models to engage in thought processes and retrieve observations from tools in an interleaved manner.
In existing ALM systems, Large Language Models first decide to utilize an external tool, pause to receive this tool's response, and then base subsequent actions on all prior response tokens.
The aforementioned paradigm for ALMs is straightforward but can lead to computation complexity due to redundant prompts and repeated execution.
This research tackles the challenges arising from the paradigm for the first time.
This paper presents a modular paradigm called ReWOO (Reasoning Without Observation) that decouples the reasoning process from external observations.
Evaluations across six public NLP benchmarks and a custom dataset show consistent performance improvements with our proposed method.
ReWOO achieves a significant token efficiency of 5x and a 4% accuracy improvement on HotpotQA, a multi-step reasoning benchmark.
ReWOO shows robustness in scenarios where tools may fail.
The practice of separating parametric modules from non-parametric tool calls allows for fine-tuning instructions to lesser language models, subsequently reducing model parameters.
Our research demonstrates the transfer of reasoning ability from 175B GPT3.5 to a 7B LLaMA model.
This shows the substantial potential for the development of efficient and scalable ALM systems.
Conversational systems based on LLMs show exceptional proficiency in context understanding and response generation.
Despite the capabilities of LLM-based conversational systems, they still possess limitations.
The limitations of LLM-based conversational systems include providing randomly-guessed answers to ambiguous queries or failing to refuse users' requests.
The question is whether LLM-based conversational systems are equipped to handle proactive dialogue problems.
In this work, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of LLM-based conversational systems.
We focus on three aspects of proactive dialogue systems: clarification, target-guided, and non-collaborative dialogues.
We propose the Proactive Chain-of-Thought prompting scheme to trigger the proactivity of LLMs.
The Proactive Chain-of-Thought prompting scheme augments LLMs with the goal planning capability over descriptive reasoning chains.
Empirical findings are discussed to promote future studies on LLM-based proactive dialogue systems.
Recently, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been successful on complex reasoning tasks.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting is designed to create a simple prompt such as "Let's think step by step" or provide multiple in-context exemplars accompanied by well-structured rationales.
The generated rationales from Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting often contain errors, leading to unfactual and unfaithful reasoning chains.
To address the brittleness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, we propose a new method called Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK) prompting.
Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK) prompting intends to encourage Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce explicit pieces of knowledge.
Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK) prompting was inspired by human behaviors, specifically the ability to create a mind map or knowledge map to represent reasoning evidence before answering a complex question.
With Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK), we introduce a new F^2-Verification method to evaluate the reliability of reasoning chains based on factuality and faithfulness.
For responses that are deemed unreliable via the F^2-Verification method, incorrect evidence can be highlighted to prompt Large Language Models (LLMs) to reconsider.
Experiments show that our proposed method can enhance the performance of commonsense, factual, symbolic, and arithmetic reasoning tasks.
A long-standing goal of AI systems is to perform complex multimodal reasoning like humans.
Recently, large language models have made remarkable strides in multi-step language-based reasoning using the chain of thought to mimic human thinking.

The transfer of advancements in language-based reasoning to multimodal contexts presents heightened challenges related to labor-intensive annotation, limited flexibility, generalizability, and explainability.

This work analyzes the challenges in multimodal CoT reasoning and presents two key insights for addressing these challenges: "keeping critical thinking"and"letting everyone do their jobs" in multimodal CoT reasoning.

This study proposes a novel DDCoT prompting strategy that maintains a critical attitude and incorporates visual recognition into reasoning processes by dividing the reasoning tasks of LLMs into reasoning and recognition, integrating the visual recognition capabilities of visual models.

The rationales generated by DDCoT significantly enhance the reasoning abilities of both large and small language models in zero-shot prompting and fine-tuning learning, outperforming state-of-the-art methods, and showing impressive generalizability and explainability.
Large language models (LLMs) are capable of performing a wide range of complex reasoning tasks with the help of prompting methods.
Current prompting methods can lead to imperfect task reduction and confusion due to the generation of natural language intermediate steps in reasoning.
We propose exploring code prompting, a neural symbolic prompting method that can trigger code as intermediate steps for reasoning, with both zero-shot and few-shot versions.
We perform experiments on 7 benchmarks that include tasks related to symbolic reasoning and arithmetic reasoning.
Code prompting typically achieves better results than chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting.
We conduct comprehensive ablation studies, error analyses, and comparisons to understand the strengths and weaknesses of code prompting, particularly in contrast to natural language prompting.
We examine the combination of code prompting and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting to leverage their respective strengths.
We investigate the impact of code annotations and their locations on code prompting through experiments.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a groundbreaking technology.
LLMs have unparalleled text generation capabilities across various applications.
Concerns persist regarding the accuracy and appropriateness of LLMs’ generated content.
A contemporary methodology, self-correction, has been proposed as a solution to the issues with LLMs’ generated content.
In the realm of reasoning, LLMs experience difficulty correcting their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance worsens after self-correction.
Based on these findings, recommendations for future research and practical applications are provided in this area.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown human-like reasoning abilities.
Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with complex logical problems.
A novel framework, Logic-LM, is introduced to improve logical problem-solving by integrating LLMs with symbolic solvers.
Our method utilizes LLMs to translate natural language problems into symbolic formulations.
After symbolic formulation, a deterministic symbolic solver performs inference.
A self-refinement module is introduced to revise symbolic formalizations based on error messages from the symbolic solver.
Logic-LM is demonstrated to be effective on five logical reasoning datasets: ProofWriter, PrOntoQA, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction, and AR-LSAT.
On average, Logic-LM achieves a significant performance boost (39.2%) over using LLM alone with standard prompting and an additional (18.4%) boost over LLM with chain-of-thought prompting.
Our findings suggest that Logic-LM is a promising approach for faithful logical reasoning by combining LLMs with symbolic logic.
The code and data for Logic-LM are made publicly available.
Task-oriented dialogue (TOD) systems facilitate users in executing various activities via multi-turn dialogues.
Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to comprehend the intricate contexts of task-oriented dialogues.
In this study, a novel prompting strategy called "Self-Explanation" is proposed to enhance the comprehension abilities of LLMs in multi-turn dialogues.
This prompting strategy, named "Self-Explanation", is task-agnostic.
The strategy requires the model to analyze each dialogue utterance before task execution, thereby potentially improving performance across various dialogue-centric tasks.
Experimental results from six benchmark datasets show that the proposed method consistently outperforms other zero-shot prompts and matches or exceeds the efficacy of few-shot prompts.
The proposed method demonstrates its potential as a powerful tool in enhancing Large Language Models' (LLMs) comprehension in complex dialogue tasks.
Recent AI-assistant agents rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT), human annotations, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
These AI-assistant agents align the output of LLMs with human intentions.
The dependence on human supervision can significantly constrain the true potential of AI-assistant agents.
There are issues with quality, reliability, diversity, self-consistency, and undesirable biases associated with human supervision.
We propose the SELF-ALIGN approach to address the challenges with human supervision.
SELF-ALIGN combines principle-driven reasoning and the generative power of LLMs for self-alignment of AI agents with minimal human supervision.
Our approach consists of four stages, with the first stage using an LLM to generate synthetic prompts and augment the prompt diversity using topic guidance.

The second stage involves using a small set of human-written principles for AI models to follow, and training the LLM to produce helpful, ethical, and reliable responses via in-context learning from demonstrations.

In the third stage, we fine-tune the original LLM using high-quality self-aligned responses so that the resulting model can generate desirable responses for each query without the need for the principle set or demonstrations.
A refinement step is included in the final stage to address issues with overly-brief or indirect responses.
Using SELF-ALIGN, we develop an AI assistant called Dromedary from the LLaMA-65b base language model.
Dromedary was developed with minimal human annotations: fewer than 300 lines, including seed prompts, generic principles, and exemplars for in-context learning.
Dromedary significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art AI systems, including Text-Davinci-003 and Alpaca, across multiple benchmark datasets and settings.

The surprising ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform well on complex reasoning with few-shot chain-of-thought prompts is primarily observed in very large-scale models with more than 100 billion parameters.
It is possible to transfer the abilities of GPT-3.5 (with at least 175 billion parameters) to smaller T5 variants (with fewer than 11 billion parameters).
We suggest a method called "model specialization" to focus the model's ability on a specific target task.
Large models, generally seen as having more than 100 billion parameters, possess strong modeling power, but their capabilities are scattered across a wide range of tasks.
Small models (commonly viewed as smaller than 10B) have limited model capacity, but if we concentrate their capacity on a specific target task, the model can achieve a decent improved performance.
We have chosen multi-step math reasoning as our benchmark, as it is a common emerging ability.

Our findings demonstrate two key aspects of language models' abilities: (1) There is a highly complex relationship/ tradeoff between the various abilities of language models; (2) By sacrificing their general capabilities, models smaller than 10 billion parameters can significantly increase their specialized multi-step math reasoning performance.
We provide detailed discussions on crucial design decisions for enhanced generalization, such as tuning data format, the initial model checkpoint, and a new selection method for models.
We hope that our methods and findings can contribute significantly to the development of specialized smaller models within the new research direction established by Large Language Models (LLMs).
Recent work has demonstrated that language models possess strong multi-step or procedural reasoning abilities.
There is uncertainty regarding whether LMs perform multi-step reasoning tasks by exploiting memorized answers from the pretraining corpus, or by employing a genuine multi-step reasoning mechanism.
In this study, we attempt to resolve the question about the mechanism behind language models' multi-step reasoning by investigating a mechanistic interpretation of LMs for multi-step reasoning tasks.
Concretely, our hypothesis is that the language model contains an implicit reasoning tree that mirrors the correct reasoning process within its structure.
We examine our hypothesis through the development of a new probing technique (MechanisticProbe) that retrieves the reasoning tree from the model's attention patterns.

We employ our probe to assess two language models: GPT-2 on a synthetic task (finding the k-th smallest element), and LLaMA on two simple language-based reasoning tasks (ProofWriter and AI2 Reasoning Challenge).

Our results demonstrate that MechanisticProbe can detect the information of the reasoning tree from the model's attentions for a majority of examples, suggesting that the language model undergoes a multi-step reasoning process within its architecture in multiple instances.
Step-by-step reasoning approaches like chain-of-thought (CoT) have proved to be an effective technique to induce reasoning capabilities in large language models.
The success of the chain-of-thought (CoT) approach depends primarily on model size, and requires billion parameter-scale models to work effectively.
In this paper, we propose a knowledge distillation approach that transfers the step-by-step reasoning capabilities of larger CoT models to smaller models.

Our approach D ECOMPOSI-TIONAL D ISTILLATION learns to decompose complex reasoning problems into a sequence of simpler subproblems, using this decomposition to train two models: a problem decomposer and a problem solver.
On the GSM8K multi-step math word problem dataset, we improve the performance of GPT-2 variants by up to 35% when trained using our approach compared to the CoT approach.
Our approach allows the training of a smaller GPT-2-large model (775M) that outperforms a larger GPT-3 (6B) model trained using the CoT approach.
Our approach of problem decomposition can also be used as an alternative to CoT prompting, which improves GPT-3 performance by 40% compared to the CoT prompting approach.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting empowers the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs).
The multi-step reasoning ability of CoT methods is limited to English due to the success of CoT methods.
There is an imbalance in the distribution of pre-training data, making other languages a barrier to multi-step reasoning.
We propose a Cross-lingual multi-step reasoning approach.
Our Cross-lingual multi-step reasoning approach aims to align the reasoning processes across different languages.
Our Cross-lingual multi-step reasoning method employs a Self-consistent Cross-lingual prompting mechanism to deliver multi-step reasoning paths in different languages.
Our Cross-lingual multi-step reasoning method generates multi-step reasoning paths in different languages that lead to the final solution.
Our experimental evaluations indicate that our Cross-lingual multi-step reasoning approach significantly outperforms existing prompting methods.
Our method reduces the number of interactions needed for multi-step reasoning.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-step reasoning.
Chain-of-Thought prompting is popular in reasoning tasks.
The application of Chain-of-Thought prompting in Natural Language Understanding (NLU) for Large Language Models (LLMs) is under-explored.
The Coarse-to-Fine Chain-of-Thought (CoF-CoT) approach is proposed to leverage multi-step reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs).
The Coarse-to-Fine Chain-of-Thought (CoF-CoT) approach breaks down Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks into multiple reasoning steps.
In these reasoning steps, LLMs can learn to acquire and leverage essential concepts.
The Coarse-to-Fine Chain-of-Thought (CoF-CoT) approach allows for solving Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks from different granularities.
We propose using semantic-based Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) structured knowledge as an intermediate step along with the Coarse-to-Fine Chain-of-Thought (CoF-CoT) approach.
The semantic-based Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) structured knowledge is utilized to capture the nuances and diverse structures of utterances.
The semantic-based Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) structured knowledge is used to understand connections between the varying levels of granularity in utterances.

Our proposed Coarse-to-Fine Chain-of-Thought (CoF-CoT) approach and the use of semantic-based Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) structured knowledge are demonstrated effective in helping Large Language Models (LLMs) adapt to multi-grained Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks.

Our proposed Coarse-to-Fine Chain-of-Thought (CoF-CoT) approach is demonstrated effective in helping Large Language Models (LLMs) adapt to multi-grained Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks under both zero-shot and few-shot multi-domain settings.
Prompting large language models has enabled significant recent progress in generating text with multi-step reasoning.
When applied to text generation from semi-structured data like graphs or tables, the methods typically suffer from low semantic coverage, hallucination, and logical inconsistency.
We propose MURMUR, a method that combines neural and symbolic components to generate multi-step reasoning text from semi-structured data like graphs or tables.

MURMUR is a method that generates reasoning paths by using (1) neural and symbolic modules with specific linguistic and logical skills, (2) a grammar that specifies valid combinations of modules, and (3) value functions to evaluate each reasoning step.
We evaluate our proposed method on two diverse data-to-text generation tasks: WebNLG and LogicNLG.
The tasks differ in the kind of data representations (graphs and tables) they use, and they cover multiple linguistic and logical skills.
MURMUR outperforms recent few-shot methods like direct prompting and chain-of-thought prompting.

In addition, human evaluation demonstrates that MURMUR generates reasoning paths that are more logically consistent than the ones generated by direct prompting, leading to a 26% increase in consistent summaries on LogicNLG.
On out-of-domain data, MURMUR achieves performance comparable to fine-tuned GPT-2.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have remarkable success but are challenging to deploy due to their large size, particularly on resource-constrained hardware.
The focus of existing LLM compression methods is on quantization rather than pruning. This is due to the high cost and challenges associated with training-based approaches and data collection.
One-shot pruning methods have become dominant in LLM pruning due to their cost-effectiveness and data-freeness, but they lead to a performance decline under the structured pruning setting.
In this work, a new method called Compresso for structurally pruning LLMs is introduced.
Our approach learns optimal pruning decisions by collaborating between the proposed resource-efficient pruning algorithm and the LLM during the training process.
Compresso addresses the challenges of expensive training costs and data collection by incorporating Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into the $L_0$ regularization during the instruction tuning process.
A collaborative prompt is introduced to foster collaboration between the LLM and the pruning algorithm, significantly improving the overall performance.
The method called Compresso successfully prunes LLaMA-7B to 5.4B, maintaining the original performance and even surpassing LLaMA-7B's performance in reading comprehension by 2.62%.

Extensive experiments show that Compresso significantly outperforms one-shot pruning baselines, with up to 2.21%, 11.43%, 7.04%, and 4.81% higher scores on the commonsense reasoning, reading comprehension, MMLU, and BBH benchmarks, respectively, across various sparsity ratios.
The ability to perform causal reasoning is considered a core feature of intelligence.
We investigate whether large language models can coherently reason about causality in this work.

Much of the existing work in NLP focuses on evaluating commonsense causal reasoning in LLMs, neglecting the assessment of whether a model can perform causal inference according to well-defined formal rules.
We propose a new NLP task, causal inference in natural language, inspired by the causal inference engine proposed by Judea Pearl et al.

We create the CLadder dataset consisting of 10,000 samples constructed by using a collection of causal graphs and queries (associational, interventional, and counterfactual) to obtain symbolic questions and corresponding ground-truth answers through an oracle causal inference engine.
The symbolic questions and ground-truth answers obtained from the oracle causal inference engine are translated into natural language.
We evaluate various LLMs using our dataset and introduce and evaluate a tailor-made chain-of-thought prompting strategy called CausalCoT.
We demonstrate that our task is highly challenging for large language models and conduct an in-depth analysis to gain insights into their causal reasoning abilities.
We make the CLadder dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/causalNLP/cladder, and our code can be found at https://github.com/causalNLP/cladder.
Progress has been made in language model research, with a focus on matching language patterns.
The focus of language model research is shifting from modeling language to emulating human-like reasoning abilities.
This work investigates the finance domain, which requires real-world, complex numerical reasoning.
A new large-scale dataset, ConvFinQA, is proposed to examine the sequence of numerical reasoning in conversational question answering.
The proposed dataset presents a significant challenge in modeling long-range, complex numerical reasoning in real-world conversations.
Comprehensive experiments and analyses are performed with both neural symbolic methods and prompting-based methods to understand the reasoning mechanisms of these two approaches.
The proposed dataset is believed to be a useful resource for advancing research in real-world, complex reasoning tasks.
The dataset and the associated code are publicly available.
The ability to perform causal reasoning is a core feature of intelligence.
In this work, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can reason coherently about causality.

Much of the existing work in natural language processing (NLP) focuses on evaluating commonsense causal reasoning of LLMs but does not assess whether a model can perform causal inference according to a set of well-defined formal rules.

To address the lack of evaluating causal inference in accordance with well-defined formal rules, we propose a new NLP task, causal inference in natural language, inspired by Judea Pearl's concept of the "causal inference engine."

We create a dataset, CL ADDER, containing 10K samples by using a collection of causal graphs and queries, generating symbolic questions and ground-truth answers with the help of an oracle causal inference engine.
The obtained symbolic questions and ground-truth answers are then translated into natural language to create a version of the dataset suitable for use with LLMs.
We evaluate multiple large language models (LLMs) on our dataset and introduce and evaluate a custom chain-of-thought prompting strategy called C AUSAL C O T.

We demonstrate that the proposed causal inference in natural language task is extremely challenging for large language models (LLMs), and we conduct a thorough analysis to better understand the causal reasoning abilities of these models.
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in recent natural language processing (NLP) tasks, but deployment poses challenges due to high computational and memory demands.
Recent studies have focused on improving smaller models using knowledge distillation from large language models (LLMs), resulting in promising outcomes.
Smaller models typically fail to replicate the performance of large language models (LLMs) in reasoning-intensive tasks.
This work presents the Mixed Distillation (MD) framework, which leverages the Program of Thought (PoT) and Chain of Thought (CoT) abilities within large language models (LLMs).
The Mixed Distillation (MD) framework combines multiple prompting techniques and transfers the Program of Thought (PoT) and Chain of Thought (CoT) abilities of LLMs into smaller models.
The Mixed Distillation (MD) framework significantly improves the single-path and multi-path reasoning of smaller models in a wide range of tasks according to experimental results.
The model generated using the Mixed Distillation (MD) framework surpasses the overall performance of two individually distilled models in terms of accuracy and applicability in reasoning tasks.
On the SVAMP benchmark, LLaMA2-7B and CodeLlama-7B with Mixed Distillation (MD) show significant performance boosts of 84.5% and 85.5%, respectively, exceeding GPT-3.5-Turbo by 2.5% and 3.5%.
This work's code and pre-trained model weights are released.
Comparative reasoning is crucial for text preference prediction.
Large language models often demonstrate inconsistencies in their comparative reasoning.
Chain-of-Thought approach improves accuracy in many settings but has difficulties consistently distinguishing the similarities and differences of complex texts.
SC is a prompting approach introduced to predict text preferences by generating structured intermediate comparisons.
SC begins by proposing aspects of comparison and generates textual comparisons under each aspect.
SC uses a pairwise consistency comparator to select consistent comparisons that clearly distinguish the differences between texts for each aspect.
SC reduces hallucination and improves consistency.
Comprehensive evaluation across various NLP tasks shows that SC equips LLMs to achieve state-of-the-art performance in text preference prediction.
Automatic coding of a patient's behaviors is essential to support decision making for psychotherapists in the context of motivational interviewing (MI).

Machine learning has been adapted to predict patient states during motivational interviewing (MI) sessions, but the lack of domain-specific knowledge and overlooking patient-therapist interactions pose major challenges in developing and deploying these models in real practice.

To address the challenges of developing and deploying machine learning models for predicting patient states during motivational interviewing (MI) and lacking domain-specific knowledge and overlooking patient-therapist interactions, we propose the Chain-of-Interaction (CoI) prompting method to contextualize large language models (LLMs) for psychiatric decision support by the dyadic interactions.

The Chain-of-Interaction (CoI) prompting approach systematically breaks down the patient behavior coding task into three key reasoning steps: extracting patient engagement, learning therapist question strategies, and integrating dyadic interactions between patients and therapists.
Our proposed Chain-of-Interaction (CoI) prompting approach enables large language models to leverage the coding scheme, patient state, and domain knowledge for patient behavioral coding.

Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our Chain-of-Interaction (CoI) prompting method with multiple state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) compared to existing prompting baselines.
We have performed extensive ablation analysis and show the critical role of dyadic interactions in applying large language models (LLMs) for understanding psychotherapy behavior.
Large pre-trained vision and language models have demonstrated remarkable capacities.
Solving the knowledge-based visual reasoning tasks remains challenging.

The challenge arises due to the requirement for a model to comprehensively understand image content, connect external world knowledge, and perform step-by-step reasoning to answer questions correctly.
The Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR) framework is proposed for few-shot knowledge-based visual reasoning.
The Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR) contains three stages, see, think, and confirm.
The see stage, in the Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR), scans the image and grounds visual concept candidates with a visual perception model.
The think stage, in the Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR), adopts a pre-trained large language model (LLM) to attend to key concepts from candidates adaptively.

The think stage, in the Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR), transforms the key concepts into text context for prompting with a visual captioning model and uses the LLM to generate the answer.

The confirm stage, in the Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR), generates supporting rationale to the answer using the LLM, verifies the generated rationale with a cross-modality classifier, and ensures the rationale can infer the predicted output consistently.
Experiments are conducted on a range of knowledge-based visual reasoning datasets.
The Interactive Prompting Visual Reasoner (IPVR) enjoys several benefits:
1. It achieves better performance than the previous few-shot learning baselines.
2. It offers total transparency and trustworthiness of the whole reasoning process through providing rationales for each reasoning step.
3. It is computation-efficient compared with other fine-tuning baselines.
The reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) are investigated with a focus on the Open Pretrained Transformers (OPT) models.

Three different sizes of the Open Pretrained Transformers (OPT) models are finetuned on a carefully curated reasoning corpus, resulting in two sets of finetuned models: OPT-R, finetuned without explanations, and OPT-RE, finetuned with explanations.
The performance of all models is evaluated on 57 out-of-domain tasks drawn from the Super-NaturalInstructions benchmark, covering 26 distinct reasoning skills.
Investigating the role of explanations on different reasoning skills is accomplished through the dimensions of finetuning, prompting, and scale and using three prompting techniques.
The impact of explanations on the performance of the models is studied through a comprehensive grid of 27 configurations and 6,156 test evaluations.
Having explanations in the fewshot exemplar has no significant impact on the model’s performance when the model is finetuned, but positively impacts the non-finetuned counterpart.
Incorporating explanations during prompting and finetuning results in a slight yet consistent increase in classification accuracy.
Insights are provided on which reasoning skills benefit the most from incorporating explanations during finetuning and prompting.
Numerical (+20.4%) and Analogical (+13.9%) reasoning skills show improvements when explanations are incorporated in the finetuning or prompting process.

For some reasoning skills, the incorporation of explanations may result in negligible or negative effects, and appropriate recommendations in the best practice are identified when incorporating explanations.
We use large language models (LLMs) to augment and accelerate research on the P versus NP problem.
We propose Socratic reasoning, a general framework that promotes in-depth thinking with LLMs for complex problem-solving.
Socratic reasoning encourages LLMs to recursively discover, solve, and integrate problems while facilitating self-evaluation and refinement.
Our pilot study on the P vs. NP problem shows that GPT-4 successfully produces a proof schema and engages in rigorous reasoning throughout 97 dialogue turns.
GPT-4 successfully concludes "P $\neq$ NP" in the pilot study on the P vs. NP problem, which is in alignment with (Xu and Zhou, 2023).
The investigation uncovers novel insights within the extensive solution space of LLMs.
The investigation sheds light on LLM for Science.
Logical reasoning is an ongoing pursuit in AI.
Large language models (LLMs) are capable of making significant advancements but struggle with complex logical reasoning problems.
Scalable oversight is a promising direction for enhancing logical reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), which involves the models identifying their own errors and improvement.
Numerous self-verification methods have been proposed for scaling oversight in logical reasoning.
It remains unclear whether existing large language models (LLMs) understand their errors well.
This paper explores the accuracy of large language models (LLMs) in identifying logical fallacies, focusing on their ability to self-verify in the context of logical reasoning.
We introduce a dataset, FALLACIES, which contains 232 types of reasoning fallacies organized in a hierarchical taxonomy.
Through a series of comprehensive and detailed experiments on the FALLACIES dataset, we analyze the verification abilities of multiple models.
Our primary findings indicate that existing large language models (LLMs) may struggle to accurately identify fallacious reasoning steps, casting doubt on the validity of self-verification methods.
Based on these findings, we propose suggestions for further research and practical applications in self-verification methods.
Existing dialogue models may generate unnatural, inappropriate, or unhelpful responses because they are not well-represented in the training data.
We propose the "Ask an Expert" framework that allows the model to consult an expert at each turn during the dialogue.
Advice from the expert is solicited via a structured dialogue and the model is optimized to selectively use or ignore it depending on the context and dialogue history.
In this work, the expert is represented by a Linear Language Model (LLM).

This framework is evaluated in a mental health support domain, and the structure of the conversations with the expert is guided by pre-defined prompts that represent the reasoning strategies taught to practitioners in this field.
The use of "Ask an Expert" framework in Blenderbot models results in quality improvements across all expert sizes, even those with fewer parameters than the dialogue model itself.
Our best model results in a $\sim 10\%$ improvement over the baselines, and it approaches human-level scores on the "engagingness" and "helpfulness" metrics.
The problem being addressed is human-machine collaboration within a collaborative building task in Minecraft.

An integrated system named Lara is presented, which utilizes advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP), Knowledge Representation, Inductive Logic Programming, Planning, and Statistical Relational AI to address the problem of human-machine collaboration in a collaborative building task in Minecraft.

The core components of the Lara system are a language parser and generator for effective communication, a rich representation based on first-order logic that allows for generalization, a concept learner that can generalize from a small number of instances with human guidance, and a planner that efficiently uses domain knowledge.
The integrated system (Lara) has been presented and demonstrated in the provided paper.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable performance on various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks.
There is a current debate regarding the reasoning capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs).
In this paper, we examine the performance of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and BARD models.
A thorough technical evaluation on different reasoning tasks across eleven distinct datasets is performed on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and BARD models.
Our paper provides empirical evidence that ChatGPT-4 outperforms both ChatGPT-3.5 and BARD in the zero-shot setting across almost all evaluated tasks.
The improvement of GPT-4 over GPT-3.5 may be due to a larger size and improved NLP efficiency.
The improvement of BARD over GPT-3.5 was not evident.
Our study shows that the three models have limited proficiency in Inductive, Mathematical, and Multi-hop Reasoning Tasks.
We provide a detailed and comprehensive analysis of the results from the three models to support our findings.
We propose a set of engineered prompts that enhance the zero-shot setting performance of all three models, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and BARD.
Clinical trials are critical for drug development.
Constructing the appropriate eligibility criteria is essential for the success of a clinical trial.
Proper design of clinical trial protocols should consider similar precedent trials and their eligibility criteria to ensure sufficient patient coverage.
This paper presents a method named AutoTrial to aid in the design of clinical eligibility criteria using language models.

AutoTrial has the ability to generate controllable output under instructions via a hybrid of discrete and neural prompting, to incorporate knowledge at scale via in-context learning, and to provide explicit reasoning chains for understanding its outputs.

Experiments on over 70K clinical trials verify that AutoTrial generates high-quality criteria texts that are fluent, coherent, and have high accuracy in capturing relevant clinical concepts to the target trial.
Our proposed method, with a much smaller parameter size, gains around 60% winning rate against the GPT-3.5 baselines according to human evaluations.
GPT-3.5 baselines lose to our method around 60% of the time in human evaluations.
